title: FLIR1: Nimitz / Tic Tac
locationPrecision: Approximate regional marker, not an encounter coordinate
locationEvidence: David Fravor's congressional testimony places the Nimitz workup off California and refers to conditions off San Diego. The marker represents that broad offshore region.
hook: A real Navy recording. A much larger witness account.
summary: The FLIR recording belongs to the November 2004 Nimitz episode later described to Congress by former Navy commander David Fravor. A targeting sensor tracks a small area of contrast through changes in display mode and magnification. The Pentagon authenticated and officially released the Navy footage in April 2020, describing its subject as unidentified. Fravor's account of a white, elongated object and striking flight behavior is separate eyewitness testimony; he says another crew made the recording after his encounter. That distinction matters: the short video cannot independently establish every maneuver described in the wider account.

title: Gimbal: the rotating image
region: Recording location not specified in the cited official release
locationPrecision: No map pin: cited primary record does not specify an encounter location
hook: The image turns. What turned with it?
summary: Gimbal is one of the three Navy videos the Pentagon officially released in April 2020. The infrared display shows a dark, apparently flattened shape that rotates within the sensor view, accompanied by crew audio. The release authenticated the footage and characterized the phenomenon as unidentified. It did not conclude that a physical craft rotated, identify the target, or publish a definitive account of its motion. The distinction between an object's behavior and the appearance produced by a moving imaging system is central to reading this clip. The cited NAVAIR catalog supplies no useful encounter coordinates, so this record has no globe pin.

facts: The Pentagon authenticated this as a Navy video and dated the 2015 clips to January.
The target's image appears to rotate within the sensor display.
The release does not identify the object or endorse a specific extraordinary explanation.
limits: An apparent rotation in infrared imagery is not by itself proof that a physical vehicle rotated. The public clip and its release statement do not establish distance, material, propulsion or origin.

title: GoFast: speed without the speed
region: Atlantic Ocean off the eastern coast of Florida
locationPrecision: Approximate regional marker, not an encounter coordinate
locationEvidence: AARO's February 2025 resolution card names the eastern coast of Florida. The marker represents that offshore region.
hook: The ocean races past. The object need not.
summary: GoFast appears to show a small object racing close to the sea. AARO's February 2025 analysis reached a different conclusion: the target was approximately 13,000 feet above the Atlantic off Florida, and the apparent rapid movement was affected by viewing geometry and parallax. Accounting for the wind, its assessed speed range was roughly 5 to 92 mph. AARO expressed high confidence that the object displayed no anomalous performance characteristics, while explicitly saying it could not definitively identify it. This is a resolution of the dramatic speed interpretation, not a complete identification of everything visible in the frame.
videoLabel: Official NAVAIR GOFAST recording, hosted by DVIDS

facts: AARO assessed an altitude of approximately 13,000 feet rather than near the sea surface.

limits: Resolved refers to the anomalous-performance claim. AARO's speed estimates depend on geometry, wind and heading assumptions; the object itself remains unidentified.

title: The Middle East sphere
locationPrecision: No map pin: the public source names only the Middle East
hook: A sphere crosses the frame. The identity stays open.
summary: An MQ-9 recorded an apparently silver, orb-like object crossing its field of view in the Middle East. AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick presented the clip at an open Senate hearing in April 2023. The official description is unusually clear about the boundary of the finding: AARO did not assess the object as exhibiting anomalous behavior, but could not identify it from the available material. It retained the case in its active archive pending additional information. The short recording is compelling because it preserves an observation while also showing how little a brief image can tell investigators about the thing being observed.

facts: An MQ-9 captured the released clip; its public record gives 12 July 2022.

limits: The exact site, size, distance and identity are not established by this public clip. A broad Middle East label is insufficient to assign the encounter to a particular country.

title: Aguadilla: the apparent sea crossing
region: Rafael Hernández Airport area, Aguadilla, Puerto Rico
locationPrecision: Approximate airport-area marker, not a reconstructed target position
locationEvidence: The CBP observation is officially placed over Rafael Hernández Airport near Aguadilla. The pin marks its general airport area, not the objects' track.
hook: One object splits and dives—or two drift over land.
summary: A Customs and Border Protection aircraft recorded infrared footage near Aguadilla that appeared to show fast movement, an object splitting, and a passage into the sea. AARO's reconstruction instead found two objects traveling together at wind speed over land, without entering the water. Its March 2025 report assessed with high confidence that there was no anomalous behavior or movement between air and water, and with moderate confidence that the targets were a pair of sky lanterns. The video remains fascinating as a demonstration of how an aircraft's changing position, distance and viewing angle can transform an ordinary track into a dramatic visual story.
videoLabel: Original CBP infrared footage, officially hosted by DVIDS

sources.label: AARO Puerto Rico resolution, 20 March 2025

facts: The original infrared footage was recorded on 26 April 2013 near Aguadilla.
AARO's reconstruction found two wind-driven objects, without a water entry.
The sky-lantern identification has moderate confidence; the non-anomalous motion finding has high confidence.
limits: AARO's reconstruction is an analytical model, not another camera view of the encounter. The probable sky-lantern identification is less certain than its finding about the objects' motion.

title: Yellow Sea: the star-shaped return
locationPrecision: Approximate sea-region marker, not an encounter coordinate
locationEvidence: The official title and DVIDS location name the Yellow Sea. The coordinates are an editorial regional marker only.
hook: A six-pointed image. No six-pointed craft established.
summary: Released in the July 2026 PURSUE collection, this short infrared recording follows an area of contrast over the Yellow Sea. AARO's official description says that its appearance resembles a six-pointed star and that the sensor pans to keep it near the center of the display. The entry remains an unresolved UAP report. Crucially, its description is not an analytical determination of the target's validity, nature or significance. A distinctive sensor return is a reason to examine an image closely; it does not establish that the physical object has that shape, or that the recording shows unusual propulsion or flight performance.

title: Gulf of Oman: the recorded screen
locationPrecision: Approximate gulf-region marker, not an encounter coordinate
locationEvidence: The official DVIDS title and location identify the Gulf of Oman. The point marks only that broad sea region.
hook: A sensor sees something. A phone records the sensor.
summary: This August 2026 release comes with a provenance detail that changes how it should be watched. PR117 is a cellphone recording of an infrared display aboard an AC-130J gunship, rather than the original sensor data. U.S. Central Command supplied the material, and AARO says it belongs to a contemporaneous sequence spanning PR117 through PR122. The accompanying report described cold-looking orbs, but the released description does not turn those reported dimensions or appearances into verified measurements. This fragment shows an area of contrast staying near the sensor's center. Its interest lies partly in the observation and partly in how much information the recording process loses.

title: Tremonton: the surviving 1952 film
locationPrecision: Approximate town-area marker; filming site not established by the cited release
locationEvidence: AARO states that Newhouse filmed near Tremonton. The coordinates identify the town area, not his camera position or the objects' positions.
hook: Seventy-four years later, the print still has limits.
summary: In July 1952, Navy warrant officer Delbert Newhouse filmed bright airborne objects near Tremonton with a handheld 16 mm camera. The film entered the Air Force's UFO investigation record and was later examined in Project Blue Book. AARO's September 2026 release digitizes a surviving print, describing its limited detail and missing fixed reference points as obstacles to a conclusive resolution. The physical record has its own mystery: after approximately 55 seconds, it switches to unrelated sewing-equipment footage. AARO says the available record does not establish how the materials were combined. An official archival release preserves this uncertainty rather than solving the original sighting.
videoLabel: Official PR159 digitization; historical lights precede unrelated footage at 00:55
mediaNotes: At approximately 00:55 the surviving print switches to unrelated sewing-equipment material. This is a new public digitization of historical footage, not a newly recorded encounter.

sources.label: AARO's original film digitization and archival provenance
PURSUE Release 06 collection

facts: The official record dates the handheld film to 2 July 1952 near Tremonton.
The available images lack detail and fixed reference points needed for a conclusive resolution.
The September 2026 digitization includes unrelated material after roughly 55 seconds.
limits: The digitization does not establish target distance, size, speed or origin. Its surviving print may be composite or reused; AARO does not establish when or how unrelated material was added.

title: Rendlesham Forest: the memo and the lights
dateLabel: Late December 1980 · Halt memo dated 13 January 1981
locationPrecision: Approximate Rendlesham Forest area; not a verified light, landing or camera position. Date is month-level because the checked archive guide describes two nights late in December.
hook: A military report survives. The cause of the lights remains disputed.
summary: US airmen reported unusual lights near RAF Woodbridge in December 1980. Deputy base commander Charles Halt later took a group into the forest and made a live tape recording; his memorandum of 13 January 1981 is preserved in the official files. That establishes a documented military report. It does not settle what caused every observation. In a 2001 parliamentary answer, the MoD said its contemporary records documented no unusual radar returns and that it had no evidence of other official USAF documentation. The reported close encounter and the limits of the surviving record must be read together.

facts: Halt’s memorandum is dated 13 January 1981 and concerns December 1980 events.

limits: The memo is evidence of what was reported, not independent verification of a landed craft. Later recollections and detailed date claims must be compared with contemporaneous records. The absence of unusual radar returns in MoD files is not proof that every observation has been explained. No verified official audio embed was located.

title: Calvine: the photograph with missing context
dateLabel: Reported 4 August 1990 · date not independently confirmed
locationPrecision: Approximate Calvine village-area marker for the reported locality. The university analysis cannot establish the photograph’s actual location; this is not a camera position.
hook: The surviving print is real. What the image depicts is unresolved.
summary: A print associated with a reported 4 August 1990 sighting near Calvine was retained by former RAF press officer Craig Lindsay and donated to Sheffield Hallam University in 2022. Photographer Andrew Robinson examined the print, related photocopies and its envelope. His 2024 report concludes that it is a genuine copy of the image considered by the MoD, with no evidence of negative or print manipulation. He also states that the print cannot independently establish its date or location and that available data cannot identify the object. Authentic photographic material is not the same as a verified extraordinary craft.

facts: The surviving Lindsay print entered Sheffield Hallam’s collection in 2022.
The 2024 analysis finds no evidence of negative or print-based manipulation.
The analyst cannot confirm the date, camera location or object’s identity from the print.
limits: This is a university-held print and research analysis, not an official finding that a classified or extraterrestrial craft was photographed. A genuine scene can include a staged or ordinary object. Size estimates depend on assumptions; the reported date and locality are not independently verified. title: West Freugh: the radar echoes left unidentified
dateLabel: April 1957 · month-level date verified in the archive guide
locationPrecision: Approximate public West Freugh range-area marker. It is not a reconstructed radar track or an exact position of an observed target.
hook: The radar report was investigated. Its conclusion did not identify the targets.
summary: In April 1957, trailer-mounted radar units associated with RAF West Freugh’s bombing range reported unusual targets. The National Archives identifies the relevant Air Ministry records, including AIR 2/18564, AIR 20/9320 and AIR 20/9321. Its briefing describes a technical report concluding that five reflecting objects remained unidentified and that several ordinary explanations were considered unlikely. This is a strong example of a documented radar investigation reaching an unresolved conclusion. It does not independently establish the targets’ construction, exceptional performance or origin, and the globe marker shows the reporting area rather than a supposed craft position.

facts: The checked official archive guides date the West Freugh radar report to April 1957.

limits: A preserved technical assessment is not proof of non-human technology or a present-day validated reconstruction of the radar returns. The checked official guides support April 1957; no exact day is asserted here without inspecting the original incident sheet. No verified official film or audio was located.
